articles.title: Endangered red squirrels thriving on British island
articles.summary: Conservationists say that, with red squirrels dwindling in the UK, Jersey is an "important refuge".
articles.body:
With growing concerns that red squirrels could soon become extinct in England , one Channel Island is a corner of the British Isles where they maintain a stronghold.

Jersey is home to a thriving red squirrel population, thanks to the complete absence of grey squirrels, which carry a virus deadly to their red cousins.

Red squirrels are endangered in the UK , with about 120,000 to 160,000 left in the wild and various projects are aiming to boost those numbers.

There have some strongholds in England , particularly islands, and 75% of the British population is in Scotland .

However, despite not being native to Jersey, Henry Glynn, an ecologist with the National Trust of Jersey, said they "really are iconic for Jersey".

He said: "When you speak to people who have come over to visit the island from the UK, a lot of them will say that one of the things they want to do whilst here is to see a red squirrel, because they're so rare and so difficult to see in large parts of the UK.

"That is actually really special for them."

Red squirrels are not native to Jersey, having been introduced in 1885.

However, Glynn described them as "naturalised", having become "assimilated into the natural environment" over many years.

The animals have previously featured in Visit Jersey tourism campaigns, including one fronted by conservationist Ben Fogle.

The National Trust of Jersey said the island wa s an "important refuge" for the red squirrel, where they were " fairly widespread ".

It said the inland valleys and woodlands were the best places to spot them.

The species is legally protected, which means it would be a criminal offence to harm them.

Nina Powell, senior animal carer at the JSPCA [Jersey Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals], said Jersey has a "good population" of squirrels and that "you can see them almost anywhere".

While the primary reason for their success is the lack of grey squirrels, Powell said they also thrived "because people look out for them".

She said: "A lot of people do support them, put out feeders and stuff like that.

"Their habitats are decreasing everywhere... but we do have quite a lot of nature reserves.

"In some places, we've got rope bridges which really help them cross the roads, and our speed limits are quite low, so that helps them as well".

She said the JSPCA had handled 50 red squirrels so far this year, including hand-raising eight babies, called kits (kittens).

She said: "We want to keep all animals as wild as possible, so we try and be as hands-off as possible.

"Some of them don't like us... some of them are quite sweet. They really do vary in personality."

Glynn agreed that their success had come in part because of the efforts of islanders.

He said: "They're really beloved amongst the local community as well. A lot of people put out squirrel feeders or love to see them in the garden.

"We get lots of reports from people who just want to tell us they've seen them because they're so happy to have them around."

articles.title: Job vacancies fall as small firms cut back on recruitment
articles.summary: Small firms cite labour costs as a key factor in scaling back hiring, the Office for National Statistics says.
articles.body:
The UK's unemployment rate has dropped to its lowest for more than year, but job vacancies have continued to fall as smaller businesses cut back on recruitment, official figures indicate.

The jobless rate fell to 4.7% in the three months to August, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said, the lowest since July last year.

However, vacancies fell by 21,000 in the three months to September to 691,000, with the ONS saying small firms were citing labour costs as a key factor in scaling back hiring.

The figures are the last official snapshot of the jobs market before the Budget, and analysts said they indicated the jobs market was showing signs of recovery despite the weakness in hiring.

ONS deputy director of labour market statistics, David Freeman, said the labour market remained "broadly flat", with the latest data showing the employment rate edging up and "a small drop in unemployment".

"The number of workers on payroll remains slightly down over the same period, though data for the most recent month suggests that might be starting to level off," he said.

"The number of vacancies has seen its largest fall since the start of the year, concentrated mainly within smaller businesses, which cite increased labour costs as a key factor."

Energy costs have risen since the Iran war began, and companies have also said that increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made it more expensive to employ staff.

The number of job vacancies fell to its lowest level in more than five years, the figures indicated, with the largest decrease in construction jobs.

Average earnings excluding bonuses rose 3.7% in the three months to August, up from 3.5% last month. Taking inflation into account, wages grew 0.8% in real terms.

Pat McFadden, the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, said the figures "show the resilience of our labour market" with the UK's employment rate "now the third highest in the G7, despite a backdrop of global uncertainty".

However, he said that "too many young people still find themselves locked out of employment".

The government is working with industry "to bring young people back into the labour market and prevent them from drifting into the welfare system", he added.

But Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said on X that "businesses can't afford to hire".

"This is what happens when you attack employers, tax jobs, and put up red tape," he said.

The latest ONS figures showed the unemployment rate for those aged 16 to 24 was 15.6% in the June to August quarter. While that was down from 16.4% in the March to May period, it was still higher than the rate of 14.6% seen in the June-to-August period last year.

Separate ONS figures have indicated that nearly one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet"

On Monday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to high levels of youth unemployment.

Ashley Webb, senior UK economist for Capital Economics, said the fall in the unemployment rate was "unexpected", and that it suggests the labour market "continues to recover".

But "with businesses' energy costs likely to fall only slowly, we still think hiring will stay subdued," he said.

Louise Murphy, senior economist at the Resolution Foundation, said the labour market "has performed poorly in recent years as the number of jobs has fallen and pay growth weakened".

But she added that the UK's "recent bout of economic resilience may finally be creating some green shoots", pointing to "rising employment levels and private sector wage growth stabilising".

The quality of ONS statistics has been criticised in recent years, with a review last year finding "deep seated" issues with the body .

The Labour Force Survey, which it uses to report payroll and employment figures, has suffered from low response rates.

In an update on Tuesday, the ONS said that response levels had improved, but that "some volatility" remained in the statistics.

articles.title: Orionid meteor shower peak: How and when to see it this week
articles.summary: Clear skies permitting, skygazers could be able to spot as many as 10-20 meteors per hour as the shower peaks this week.
articles.body:
The Orionid meteor shower, which is capable of producing bright fireball meteors, is set to peak in UK skies this week.

While it has been active for most of October, the celestial spectacle will be at its best in the early hours of October 22.

Clear skies permitting, skygazers could be able to spot as many as 10-20 meteors per hour.

Where the weather is less cooperative, there will still be chances to catch a glimpse of the shower until 7 November.

Where do the Orionids come from and how can I watch them?

The Orionids are an annual meteor shower caused by debris left by Halley's comet in its journey around the Sun.

Every year, Earth passes through the comet dust and the debris burns with the friction caused by the atmosphere, creating a bright streak of light through the sky.

The Orionids are fast and bright, entering our atmosphere with speeds of around 41 miles per second. They can often produce long glowing trails and fireballs.

To spot them, find a dark spot with wide open skies, away from city light pollution and let your eyes adjust to the night sky for 20 minutes.

The meteors are visible to the naked eye so you won't need any specialist equipment like binoculars or a telescope.

The meteors will appear to originate from the constellation of Orion, near the red supergiant star Betelgeuse. This is known as the radiant.

Between midnight and dawn the constellation will climb higher in the sky to the south and then the south-west.

It is best to view the meteors slightly away from the radiant as they will be more visible.

Unfortunately, the Moon will be in the waxing gibbous phase on the night of the 21 October, throwing extra light into the night sky and reducing visibility.

However, conditions will improve once the Moon sets around 03:00 BST on Thursday morning.

Meteor showers are best seen in cloudless skies. Unfortunately for skywatchers, this week looks to be the wettest and windiest week so far this autumn with a strengthening jet stream propelling low pressure systems across the UK.

While Wednesday is looking wet and windy for many parts of the UK, a brief ridge of high pressure could mean that there is a chance of clear spells for many parts of England, Wales and Northern Ireland for the second half of the night into Thursday morning.

There may also be some clear skies for a time for western Scotland.

Eastern Scotland looks cloudy and wet with a lingering front and the far south coast of England could also see outbreaks of rain.

articles.title: In 2020, Jon Bon Jovi and his wife helped open a restaurant at Rutgers–Newark; five years later, it had served more than 14,000 meals to students, faculty and neighbours, regardless of ability to pay
articles.summary: A restaurant built around the idea that nobody should have to choose between eating and meeting other financial obligations has marked five years of
articles.body: A restaurant built around the idea that nobody should have to choose between eating and meeting other financial obligations has marked five years of serving the Rutgers University–Newark community. According to Rutgers University–Newark, the JBJ Soul Foundation and JBJ Soul Kitchen, the restaurant, founded by musician Jon Bon Jovi and his wife, Dorothea Bongiovi, has served more than 14,000 meals to students, university staff and local residents since opening on campus in 2020. Located inside the Paul Robeson Campus Center, the restaurant was established to address food insecurity through a community dining model that allows people to eat regardless of their ability to pay. The milestone was celebrated on November 10, 2025, when Rutgers–Newark and the JBJ Soul Foundation hosted a special lunch at the restaurant. The initiative reflects a growing recognition that hunger can affect college students as well as families facing financial hardship. By making nutritious meals accessible without a fixed menu price, the restaurant aims to ensure that financial difficulties do not become an additional barrier to education.A restaurant where meals are not tied to incomeUnlike conventional restaurants, JBJ Soul Kitchen operates on a pay-it-forward model. Guests can make a suggested donation towards their meal, helping support the restaurant and its mission. Those unable to contribute can still eat and are encouraged to participate in community activities, including volunteering.Each meal includes three courses prepared by chefs, with an emphasis on providing nutritious food in a welcoming setting. The model allows paying guests to help cover the cost of meals for people experiencing food insecurity, bringing together diners with different financial circumstances around the same table.According to Rutgers–Newark’s anniversary announcement, more than half of the guests served by the campus restaurant are now people in need. The figure points to the continuing demand for affordable food assistance among the university community and nearby residents.For students managing tuition, housing, transport and other living expenses, access to a dependable meal can make a meaningful difference. The restaurant’s approach also seeks to reduce the stigma sometimes associated with seeking food assistance by creating a shared dining space rather than separating those receiving support from other guests.A partnership built around student well-beingThe restaurant is the result of a partnership between the JBJ Soul Foundation, Rutgers–Newark and Gourmet Dining, the food service provider involved in its operations. University leaders have presented the initiative as an example of how institutions can work with community organisations to address needs that extend beyond the classroom.The restaurant’s work is also supported by local organisations and campus groups, including the Newark Teachers Association, the Rutgers Police Department, Students Organized Rutgers Against Hunger, and RU-N Pantry+. Their involvement helps raise awareness about food insecurity and connect students with food assistance and other resources.The collaboration is important because food insecurity is not always immediately visible on a university campus. Students may attend classes and maintain their academic responsibilities while struggling to afford regular, nutritious meals. Initiatives such as JBJ Soul Kitchen offer an additional source of support while helping build connections between students, staff and the surrounding community.Extending a mission beyond the campusThe Rutgers–Newark restaurant is part of a broader effort by the JBJ Soul Foundation to tackle hunger, homelessness and poverty. Established in 2006, the foundation supports community-based initiatives intended to improve access to essential resources and create more stable living conditions.JBJ Soul Kitchen expanded that work by developing community restaurants where people can share meals without the pressure of a fixed price. Its network includes locations in New Jersey, with the university restaurant extending the model into higher education.Five years after opening, the Rutgers–Newark branch has demonstrated how a campus dining space can serve a wider purpose. Its more than 14,000 meals represent not only food provided but also an ongoing effort to make support accessible without compromising the dignity of those who need it. As the restaurant continues its work, its central principle remains straightforward: access to a nourishing meal should not depend on how much money someone has in their pocket.In 2020, Jon Bon Jovi and his wife helped open a restaurant at Rutgers–Newark; five years later, it had served more than 14,000 meals to students, faculty and neighbours, regardless of ability to payYou use AI every day. articles.title: A Cold War missile base in Kansas has a silo plunging 182 feet underground; owners converted its neighbouring command centre into 2,500 square feet of living space, and the 18.2-acre site now asks $1.6 million
articles.summary: A former Cold War missile installation in Kansas, designed to protect a nuclear weapon deep underground, is being offered for $1.6 million after its
articles.body: A former Cold War missile installation in Kansas, designed to protect a nuclear weapon deep underground, is being offered for $1.6 million after its launch control centre was converted into living space. According to Realtor.com, which reported on the listing on October 17, 2026, the North Star Missile Silo near Carlton spans 18.2 acres and contains a 182-foot-deep silo, steel blast doors and a two-storey command centre. The property is listed for $1,600,500, with approximately 2,500 square feet of finished space in the former launch control centre.The property, also identified as Atlas F Site 550-4, offers a glimpse into the infrastructure built during a period when the United States and the Soviet Union were locked in a nuclear arms race. What was once a military installation designed for a strategic weapon has since been adapted for private use, with a living area, kitchens, bedrooms and modern utilities occupying part of the underground complex.From nuclear installation to underground homeThe North Star Missile Silo's original structure was built around the demands of nuclear-era military readiness. Its website describes a silo measuring 52 feet across and 182 feet deep, with reinforced concrete walls six feet thick. Heavy steel blast doors and underground passages connect different parts of the complex, including the launch control centre. These specifications are published on the property's own website and should be understood as its stated dimensions and features.The launch control centre has been converted into approximately 2,500 square feet of living space. According to Realtor.com, a 40-foot tunnel connects it to the silo. The finished area includes an open-plan living room and dining area, two kitchens, two bedrooms and two bathrooms, arranged across two levels.The conversion was not completed when the current owners acquired the property. Listing agent Ali Schneider of Real Broker told Realtor.com that the sellers had owned the company that held the property and had used the site as a rental. Schneider said it was not habitable when they bought it, but they subsequently finished the interior and made it functional.The property is equipped with 200-amp electrical service and metered water supplied through a rural district system. Its specifications also list separate sewer systems for the surface and underground areas, a humidity-control system, a mobile-phone signal repeater and access to high-speed fibre internet.Above ground, the 18.2-acre parcel is enclosed by barbed-wire fencing and accessed through a wide driveway from a paved road. A solar-powered, seven-foot chain-link gate with a remote keypad controls the entrance. The site also has an aluminium carport and a concrete pad with utility connections that could accommodate a recreational vehicle, according to the listing.A remnant of the Cold War missile programmeThe installation's history is tied to the Atlas F intercontinental ballistic missile programme. Atlas missiles formed part of the United States' early land-based nuclear deterrent, developed as Washington and Moscow competed to build weapons capable of striking targets across continents.The Military Standard's history of Atlas F Site 550-4 identifies it as a launch facility associated with the 550th Strategic Missile Squadron and Schilling Air Force Base in Kansas. Its records state that the site became operational in 1962 and was deactivated on March 25, 1965. The squadron itself was discontinued later that year.Atlas F installations were designed to house and support missiles in hardened underground facilities. Their engineering reflected the military's effort to protect strategic weapons and supporting equipment from attack while maintaining the ability to launch them when ordered. The sites included more than the missile shaft alone: access passages, control areas, utilities and support infrastructure were also essential to their operation.The Atlas system's active service was relatively brief. By the mid-1960s, the United States was moving away from its first-generation Atlas missiles towards newer missile systems. The deactivation of the Kansas installation marked the end of its role as an operational launch facility, although the physical structures remained.What the $1.6 million listing offersThe present-day property combines the remains of that military infrastructure with features intended for contemporary use. The listing describes room for gardening, agriculture and grazing, along with potential space for solar panels or wind turbines. Its elevated setting is advertised as offering views extending roughly 20 miles, while the fenced boundaries provide privacy.Schneider told Realtor.com that possible future uses discussed for the site include an off-grid conference venue or wedding venue. There has also been discussion about converting the silo into condominiums, although these are possibilities rather than approved projects or confirmed plans. The agent said she hoped the next buyer would preserve its history and continue using it as a rental.The property's unusual design may attract buyers seeking a distinctive residence, private retreat or investment project, but its underground structures also present considerations beyond those of an ordinary home. Prospective buyers would need to assess the condition of the silo, the suitability of the converted space, the maintenance requirements of the underground systems and the permissions needed for any proposed change of use.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: US spent $861 million on agricultural pest inspections in 2011, but legal limits and fee collection failures left a $325 million funding gap
articles.summary: In 2011, the United States spent $861 million inspecting travellers and cargo for agricultural pests, but fees collected left a shortfall of more than
articles.body: In 2011, the United States spent $861 million inspecting travellers and cargo for agricultural pests, but fees collected left a shortfall of more than $325 million. The funding gap stemmed partly from federal laws restricting which passengers and transport operators could be charged, alongside weaknesses in fee collection and differences between agency costs and revenue. According to the Government Accountability Office (GAO), the programme, jointly administered by the US Department of Agriculture and Customs and Border Protection, aims to intercept foreign agricultural pests and prevent prohibited materials from entering the country. Later reforms addressed some gaps, but legal restrictions remained.Why did US agricultural inspection fees fall short of costsThe GAO identified restrictions on the government’s fee-setting authority as one of the reasons for the shortfall. APHIS could not charge every person entering the United States, including pedestrians, under its authority. The agency was unable to recover the costs of those inspections by charging other parties. The report further identified commercial buses, private vessels and private aircraft as categories for which the existing legal framework restricted the collection of fees to cover passenger inspection costs.APHIS also chose not to charge certain passenger groups, citing difficulties associated with collecting small fees. These limitations meant that some inspection costs continued to be covered through federal appropriations rather than user fees. The GAO stated that additional legal authority would be necessary to recover all programme costs through fees. In its recommendations to Congress, the agency called for changes that would allow the Secretary of Agriculture to set rates covering the programme’s aggregate estimated costs and extend fee authority to additional transport categories.Why did CBP receive only 60% of fees despite covering over 80% of costsThe report also identified a mismatch between the costs incurred by the two agencies and the revenue they received. In 2005, APHIS and CBP had agreed to distribute AQI fee collections in proportion to each agency’s share of programme costs. However, the GAO found that this arrangement was not reflected in the fiscal year 2011 figures. CBP incurred more than 80% of total programme costs but received only 60% of fee collections. APHIS, meanwhile, incurred 19% of costs and retained 36% of collections.CBP covered the difference between its AQI expenditure and its share of fee revenues through its annual appropriation. APHIS also carried forward part of its fee collections to maintain a shared reserve with CBP against unexpected declines in revenue. According to the GAO, APHIS aimed to maintain a reserve equivalent to three to five months of programme costs, but its preliminary fee proposal would have funded the reserve above the five-month maximum. The report warned that this level would increase reliance on appropriated funds to meet current programme costs.How did missed railcar fees cost the US $13.2 million in 2010The GAO found that weaknesses in collection procedures also contributed to the funding problem. APHIS did not collect AQI fees for railcars in accordance with its regulations, resulting in a reported revenue loss of $13.2 million in 2010. CBP, meanwhile, did not verify that all fees due for commercial trucks, private aircraft and private vessels had been collected. The report said the resulting annual revenue loss for these categories was unknown.The report noted that CBP had tools available to address these collection problems but did not require their use. It recommended improvements to oversight and the allocation of inspection costs, including clearer guidance on recording officers’ work. The GAO also recommended that APHIS account for costs incurred by other federal agencies on behalf of the AQI programme when setting fees. These measures were intended to improve revenue collection and bring the distribution of fees closer to the actual costs of providing inspections.Why did US agricultural inspection fees remain insufficientIn October 2015, APHIS published a final rule introducing new AQI fee categories and adjusting existing rates. According to the GAO’s report update, the changes were intended to recover the full costs of related inspection services, including costs borne by other federal agencies. The changes included a $1.75 fee per cruise ship ticket for tickets purchased from 28 December 2015. The revised rules also removed caps on commercial cargo vessel and railcar fees and adjusted truck fees to better reflect inspection costs while retaining an incentive for trucks to use transponders.However, the changes did not eliminate every funding gap. The GAO’s update, dated February 2026, stated that Congress had not passed legislation giving the Secretary of Agriculture authority to set fees that fully recover the aggregate costs of AQI services. Rail passengers also continued to be exempt from AQI fees under the 2015 rule, leaving their inspection costs to be covered through CBP’s Salaries and Expenses appropriation. The GAO’s findings therefore identify both legal restrictions and administrative weaknesses as factors affecting the programme’s ability to fund agricultural inspections through fees.You use AI every day. articles.title: Can one photo of your face reveal how ill you are?
articles.summary: AI may help doctors judge how ill a patient is using a single photograph of their face, say US researchers.
articles.body:
An AI tool may be able to help doctors judge how ill a patient is using a single photograph of their face, say US researchers.

Trained on millions of healthy faces, and 35,000 photos of cancer patients, the tool can make estimates on survival by looking closely at features near the eyes, the scientists say.

While it's a long way from being suitable for use in hospitals, the researchers say their goal is to help doctors recommend the right treatments for their patients.

The preliminary findings are published in the Lancet Digital Health journal.

The 'FaceSurvival' AI tool suggests the area under the eyes and around the bridge of the nose are the most vital parts of the face to assess when estimating how long they might have left to live.

These metrics applied across many different types of cancers, varying in severity, including ones that had spread to the patient's bones or brain.

Most of the cancer patients, who were from the US and the Netherlands, were in their 50s or 60s, but some were children, while others were in their 90s.

Doctors already examine patients and run comprehensive checks and tests to judge how unwell they are, and what their prognosis might be.

The AI tool, which has a patent application pending, is designed to help doctors doing this work, not replace them.

Lead researcher Dr Raymond Mak, from Mass General Brigham in Boston, explained: "As the population ages, physicians need better ways to estimate physical reserve and frailty before recommending intensive treatments such as radiation, surgery or systemic therapy.

"Our goal is to make face photograph-based health assessment more quantitative, consistent and scalable so it can support personalised treatment decisions rather than replace physician judgment."

Collagen: Do you drink it? Inject it? Rub it on your skin? And does it work?

Why doing a mix of exercise could be the key to longer life

Can two hours of strength training a week reduce the risk of dying early?

Mak and colleagues are also evaluating an AI tool for predicting biological age, or how old someone looks, as opposed to their birthday age.

The 'FaceAge' tool suggests the skin below the nose and near the mouth - the so-called nasolabial folds and marionette lines - plus the forehead (frown lines), temples (crows' feet) and cheeks are a good indicator of how fast we age.

Some lifestyle habits can speed that process up, like heavy alcohol use, drug use and smoking.

Mak says the tool was "surprisingly consistent" across common real-world photos despite variations in pose, lighting, facial expression and make-up.

"It was also stable across most tested plastic surgery procedures, with only a small shift observed after rhinoplasty [a nose job]," he says.

But the researchers stress they need much more data and photos of faces, particularly from lots of different ethnic groups, to determine how well the tools work. They are still very much under development.

The research team is inviting the public to take part and receive a personalised biological age estimate by uploading their own facial photo the research team.

Prof Miroslaw Bober, an expert in video processing and machine learning at the University of Surrey in the UK, says any claims that the tool could track ageing or lifestyle changes over time would be "premature".

"This is a promising proof of concept, but it is not ready for clinical use," he said.

"The tool still needs testing against doctors' own judgement and across different hospitals and patient groups."

And he warned: "Predicting an outcome is not the same as explaining it."

articles.title: US plans balloon swarms for future wars as India advances Rs 15,000-crore stratospheric airship programme
articles.summary: The US Army is exploring the deployment of hundreds of high-altitude balloons in a future European conflict to monitor enemy movements, maintain
articles.body: The US Army is exploring the deployment of hundreds of high-altitude balloons in a future European conflict to monitor enemy movements, maintain communications, deceive air defences and potentially launch drones, highlighting the growing military significance of the stratosphere. India, meanwhile, is developing its own high-altitude airship capability under a Rs 15,000-crore programme aimed at providing persistent surveillance along its borders.The US Army's plan envisages deploying 200 to 300 balloons at a time, with hundreds or potentially thousands operating towards adversary territory during a major conflict. The platforms could carry reconnaissance equipment, electronic sensors and communications payloads, while some could deploy drones for surveillance, electronic warfare or strikes. Their role would extend beyond intelligence gathering to providing alternative communication links if satellites are disrupted or destroyed during hostilities.The US Army has been testing high-altitude balloon technology in Europe, including launches in the Baltic region and Poland, as it assesses the platforms for future multi-domain operations. Operating at altitudes of around 60,000 feet or higher, the balloons could carry cameras, radar and electronic intelligence equipment to monitor large areas. Depending on their design, they could remain airborne for days, weeks or months, although weather conditions and seasonal winds would influence their deployment.India is pursuing a related capability through its Airship-based High Altitude Pseudo Satellite programme. The Defence Acquisition Council cleared the programme in February 2026, following which the defence ministry invited domestic companies to develop the platforms under the Make-I category. The government will fund up to 70% of prototype development costs.Designed to operate at around 20 km, or 65,000 feet, the Indian airships are expected to provide persistent intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance over border regions, alongside communications support. These lighter than air vehicles are expected to carry payloads such as electro-optical and thermal imaging systems to keep an eye on the intended targets, as well as electronic intelligence equipment to snoop on the adversary's radio signals and other electro-magnetic emissions such as radars. Unlike free-floating balloons, airships offer greater control over where they can fly, thus allowing them to remain over areas of operational interest. They could monitor the adversary's military movements, while complementing satellites, drones and crewed surveillance aircraft.The programme is part of India's broader effort to shorten the sensor-to-shooter chain, enabling faster detection, tracking and sharing of target information with operational units.For both countries, stratospheric platforms offer an additional layer between conventional aerial means and satellites. The operational effectiveness of these platforms will depend on endurance, payload capacity, communications resilience and survivability in contested environments.

articles.title: Broadband blackout for thousands in Thurnscoe after cable theft
articles.summary: A police investigation is launched after the latest round of cable theft in South Yorkshire.
articles.body:
Cable thieves left thousands in a South Yorkshire village without broadband and telephone connections for two days.

People living in Thurnscoe and surrounding areas said elderly relatives were left cut off and with no other means of contacting their loved ones due to the disruption on Friday and Saturday.

South Yorkshire Police said it had received reports of manhole covers on Nicholas Lane in Goldthorpe being stolen on Friday morning, with wiring damaged in the area. An investigation was under way, a spokesperson added.

An Openreach spokesperson said: "We're sorry to everyone who was affected. Cable theft is a serious crime and can have a significant impact on communities."

The spokesperson said engineers "worked as quickly as possible to repair the extensive damage".

As well as homes, businesses were also affected.

Luke Wheat, Reform UK councillor for the Dearne North Ward, which was affected, said: "The impact of this mindless criminal theft is still rippling through our community.

"For many of our elderly and vulnerable residents, this is their only means of connection to the outside world."

He added: "Those responsible are a disgrace to society and should hang their heads in shame."

Wheat said he would write to the Mayor of South Yorkshire, Oliver Coppard, and local MPs "to demand stronger policing and action to stop more communities falling victim to this senseless criminality".

As well as the problems in Thurnscoe and surrounding areas, residents in Carcroft, Doncaster were also reportedly left without wi-fi and telephone connections last week due to cable thefts.

Insp Alison Carr said there had been a "spike" in cable thefts across Doncaster since the start of summer.

"Since the beginning of the spike we have recovered over £1m worth of copper cables from the Doncaster area," she said.

"This figure only pertains to the weight of the copper inserts within these cables, not the money it takes to install the cable and repair the areas where they are taken from."

Carr said cable theft was a "threat to public safety", adding: "These cables are often found around key infrastructure points like traffic lights and phone lines, which causes significant problems when they are removed."

articles.title: After salvage crews recovered a Wells Fargo treasure-box lid from the wreck of the S.S. Central America, it sold for $99,600 at auction in 2022
articles.summary: Discover the historic Wells Fargo treasure box lid recovered from the S.S. Central America wreck, auctioned for $99,600 in 2022. Learn about the ship's journey, its significance, and the artifacts recovered from the ocean depths.
articles.body: In the 1850s, steamships carried California gold across the Isthmus of Panama and on to New York, and one of those ships, the S.S. Central America, never completed the final leg of its journey from Havana. The ship sank during a hurricane, taking most of the people aboard and a heavy load of California gold with it. For more than a century, the ship and its cargo remained on the ocean floor, out of reach of researchers and treasure hunters. Modern salvage teams found the ship and retrieved some of its gold, personal effects, and cargo pieces. Among these items that have since been sold to collectors is a wooden lid of a treasure box belonging to Wells Fargo.A hurricane sank the Central America in September 1857The reanalysis notes from the Hurricane Research Division at NOAA for the 1857 season refer to the storm as the Central America Disaster of 1857, as documented in Ludlum’s 1963 book. This note uses a central pressure of 961 millibars as the measure of the intensity of the storm, but the wind speed of 94 knots is to be considered an estimate unless there is a specific meteorological source. The official track uses 90 knots, which the reviewers see as proof that the storm can be classified as a hurricane. The Papers of Abraham Lincoln project records that the S.S. Central America, carrying $1.5 million in gold bullion, went down off the coast of South Carolina on September 12, 1857, after being battered by the hurricane. Other information about the storm’s path and intensity includes its path near the Keys and into the Gulf, as well as being considered a major hurricane in the reanalysis, as the reviewers state that the 90-knot estimate qualifies it as such.A 1985 probability distribution guided the search that located the wreckThe wreck remained lost until a statistically based search plan led searchers to it. In Search for the SS Central America: Mathematical Treasure Hunting, published in 1992 in Interfaces, Lawrence D. Stone describes being asked in 1985 to develop a probability distribution for the ship’s location. He writes that the method combined historical, statistical, analytic, and subjective approaches and that the resulting search plan found the wreck. The paper reports that 425 people died in the sinking and describes the wreck as lying almost 8,000 feet below the surface, an approximate figure, while the 2022 auction report and numismatic sources give about 7,200 feet.The above-mentioned study reports that the Columbus-America Discovery Group raised one ton of gold bars and coins from the wreck in 1989 after three summers of effort at sea. In a 2017 interview with The Naked Scientists, Stone said that one of the key pieces of information was the last position Captain Herndon called out to a passing ship at about 6 p.m. on the evening of the sinking, roughly two hours before the vessel went down.Eastern bankers had counted on the gold as the Panic of 1857 took holdThe Lincoln project entry explains why the cargo mattered beyond its value. Eastern bankers had hoped California gold would help strengthen the financial system, and the ship’s loss came as the Panic of 1857 took hold. The scholarly picture is more layered. In The Panic of 1857: Origins, Transmission, and Containment, published in The Journal of Economic History, Charles Calomiris and Larry Schweikart trace the panic to a decline in western land and railroad investments, which stressed securities brokers and banks in eastern cities.Because the authors place the weight on those investments, and the panic was already underway before the ship sank, the lost gold appears to have worsened an already strained system rather than created the crisis. The authors describe the shock spreading through the banking system as brokers marked down collateral, margin calls intensified, and eastern money markets tightened before the Central America was lost.Holabird sold 270 recovered artifacts in Reno on December 3, 2022A December 8, 2022 press release from Ken Hall Public Relations says Holabird Western Americana Collections sold 270 lots of California Gold Rush items salvaged from the S.S. Central America at its December 3 auction in Reno, Nevada, and online. The release adds that sales reached almost $1 million, with more than 7,500 bidders from the United States and six other countries. The salvage company that discovered the wreck reached an agreement with the insurers and their successors. Coin World reported that an Ohio judge approved an agreement under which California Gold Marketing Group bought the treasure recovered in 2014 from Recovery Limited Partnership and Columbus Exploration for $30 million.The lid engraved with the Wells Fargo name brought $99,600The unique wooden lid of a Wells Fargo & Co. treasure box was among the highest-priced pieces in the auction, selling for $99,600. Holabird describes it as the lid to the oldest known Wells Fargo treasure shipment box, with the engraving “Wells Fargo & Co./New York” clearly visible. In the announcement of the December 2022 auction by Holabird Western Americana Collections, it was stated that the purser’s keys to the treasure room of the S.S. Central America were sold for $103,200 and five-button miner’s work pants found in the wreckage were sold for $114,000. Although the announcement says that it is a record of the highest price of jeans, it is worth noting that this record claim should be attributed to the organizers of the auction. A treasure shipment box from the San Francisco bankers Sather & Church sold for $6,300, CoinWeek reported.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Watch: Burning e-bikes turned into bonfires as France reels from violent protests
articles.summary: Paris has witnessed scenes of violence as protests over rising living costs and underfunded public services spread across France.
articles.body: Paris has witnessed scenes of violence as protests over rising living costs and underfunded public services spread across France. The unrest has turned violent in several cities, with the French capital emerging as one of the main flashpoints.Amid the chaos, burning electric bikes have become a common sight on Paris streets.Black smoke and flames rose from piles of e-bikes over the weekend, while one protester was seen throwing an electric bike onto a burning car.Videos from chaos-hit areas of the French capital showed plumes of smoke rising from the streets, with debris and charred remains scattered across the roads.The violence has also caused major damage to shared bicycle and scooter operators, with hundreds of vehicles destroyed or damaged during the nationwide protests.Hundreds of e-bikes and scooters damagedShared-mobility operator Dott told Reuters on Monday that around 300 of its electric bikes were destroyed and another 120 were severely damaged in Paris during Saturday’s protests. The company operates around 6,000 bikes in the French capital.Dott also reported that 80 vehicles, including bikes and scooters, were destroyed in Bordeaux, while 30 to 40 scooters were damaged in Lyon. The company estimated the total damage at around €400,000 ($450,000).Another operator, Lime, said some of its shared bicycles and scooters in Paris were destroyed or damaged during the unrest. The company estimated that it had lost around 6% of its Paris fleet.Ahead of the demonstrations, Lime said it had worked with police to remove vehicles from designated protest routes. It also restricted parking and riding in several high-risk areas, adjusting the measures over the weekend as the situation developed.Smovengo, which operates Paris’s Vélib’ Métropole bike-sharing service, told Reuters that around 300 bikes from its fleet of approximately 20,000 were damaged or stolen during the weekend unrest. Unlike other shared bikes, its vehicles are kept at docking stations rather than parked freely on pavements.Why are e-bikes catching fire during the riots?Electric bikes often use lithium-ion batteries, which can catch fire and produce intense heat and toxic smoke. Such fires can spread quickly, making burning e-bikes a potential safety hazard during violent protests.There is no indication that shared-bike operators were specifically targeted during the demonstrations over the cost of living and public services.However, thousands of bicycles are available across Paris, both on streets and at docking stations. This has made them easily accessible to protesters, who have used them to build barricades or set them on fire.France sees widespread rioting and lootingFrance experienced some of its worst unrest in years over the weekend as protests over rising living costs and underfunded public services escalated into riots and looting.In Limoges, the town hall was set on fire, while more than 3,000 shops were looted or damaged, according to the government. Violent groups also clashed with police in several cities.Authorities arrested around 2,400 people over the weekend. Police investigators are examining online videos and images to identify those involved in looting and other acts of violence.The Macron government is also considering partial curfews in some municipalities to prevent further unrest. Officials have said police numbers will be increased, particularly if protests resume next weekend, though the government has not specified how many additional officers will be deployed.France tightens security after weekend violenceFrench authorities are tightening security measures after the protests escalated into rioting, arson and looting across several cities.Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Monday that he had asked local authorities to impose limited, localised curfews to prevent further violence. President Emmanuel Macron ordered a review of security failures and rejected the resignation of Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez.The government has acknowledged shortcomings in anticipating the unrest and promised changes to policing, alongside investigations to identify those responsible for the violence.European governments have also issued travel advisories urging their citizens in France to avoid demonstrations and large gatherings amid concerns over further unrest.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2018, former WWE star Ronda Rousey bought a 4.55-acre California horse property for $765,000; six years later, it sold for $912,500
articles.summary: Ronda Rousey bought her California equestrian property in 2018 for $765,000 and sold it for $912,500 in October 2024. Discover the unique features and market journey of this 4.55-acre estate.
articles.body: A horse-oriented property gives you a little something that a normal suburban house can’t, which is space to be outside, privacy and a better connection to the surrounding countryside. A mountain property in Southern California provided that kind of escape from her public profession for former UFC champion and WWE star Ronda Rousey. Rousey purchased the 4.55-acre property in Running Springs, California, for $765,000 in June 2018. The house came back on the market in 2024, priced at $1.1 million until the asking price was cut to $999,999. The final sale price came in below the reduced asking price. Rousey bought the property in 2018 for $765,000, and it sold on October 7, 2024, for $912,500, roughly six years after her purchase. Although the sale price exceeded what she paid, the difference does not account for ownership costs, renovations or selling expenses.At the Equestrian EstateThe house is located in Rimwood Ranch, an equestrian community in Running Springs in the San Bernardino Mountains. The lot is 4.55 acres and has a two-story house built in 1993 with four bedrooms, four bathrooms and roughly 3,711 square feet of interior space. The ad defines the home as an equestrian property with an open-concept living area and new interiors. Its size and location distinguish it from a conventional residential lot, with area for outdoor use and mountain views from the back deck.Inside, the kitchen, dining room and family room connect through an open layout. The kitchen features granite countertops, a central island, a breakfast bar and stainless-steel appliances. The sunken family room has a fireplace and glass doors that open to a large back porch overlooking the mountains and woods.The master suite features a fireplace, sitting area, walk-in closet and a bath with double vanities, a jacuzzi tub and a glass-enclosed shower. Another flexible living space is the loft-style game room with a built-in wet bar, and there’s room for vehicles and storage in the three-car garage. The property's appeal also comes from its equestrian setting. The listing highlighted the mountain community, nearby horse paths, hiking and other outdoor recreation. Together, these features distinguish it from homes valued primarily for their interior space.From the original purchase to the final salePublic property records show Rousey bought the property in June 2018 for $765,000. The home was put back on the market in April 2024 for $1.1 million, around six years after it was purchased. In June 2024, the asking price was dropped to $999,999. The property went pending in August; however, the selling price listed is not the price that was finally recorded as the final sale. The sale closed on October 7, 2024, for $912,500, according to the recorded property history. That was $87,499 less than the $999,999 asking price and $187,500 less than the original $1.1 million listed price.This distinction is important when talking about the appraisal of a home. The asking price is what the seller wants to sell for. The closing price is the price at which the sale is finalised. A listing can get attention at one price and sell for another after haggling. Rousey sold the property for $912,500, which was $147,500 more than the $765,000 she paid in 2018. That represents a 19.3% increase in the recorded price over roughly six years. However, the difference is not her net profit because the available figures do not account for renovations, property taxes, insurance, maintenance, financing or real estate commissions.What the property sale showsThere are elements of the home that can appeal to a certain type of buyer: large acreage, a four-bedroom residence, outdoor vistas and an equestrian environment. The concept also included the normal trappings of a house. A big kitchen, many fireplaces, a game room and a three-car garage. Those attributes might have been why the property was touted as more than merely a mountain residence. But the eventual transaction also indicates that a listing price is no guarantee of what a home will get. The asking price was decreased during the marketing time, and the final closing came in under the close-to-$1 million barrier.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Israel's far right find fertile ground among first-time voters
articles.summary: More than half a million young people will cast their ballots in Israel next week - and they could make all the difference.
articles.body:
When Israel's far-right National Security Minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, reached voting age, he was rejected from Israel's army for being too politically extreme.

His views have not changed much in the 30 years since then - but Israel has. Once shunned by the political establishment, he is now part of the government's inner sanctum of ministers.

On the campaign trail ahead of Israel's general elections next week, Ben Gvir is often surrounded by a jubilant pack of fresh-faced young fans, waving huge party flags over the heads of his numerous security guards.

At the covered market in Ramle - a mixed city of Jewish and Arab Israelis - he told us his message to young voters was to get out and vote.

"We see the support, we see the love [and] we want to win!" he said.

More than half a million first-time voters will cast their ballots in this election, which many Israelis see as existential for Israel's future security and identity.

Polls suggest it will be a tight race, and the new young voters could help decide the result.

More than 16% are planning to support far-right parties - either Ben Gvir's Jewish Power or the Religious Zionism party of his far-right ally Bezalel Smotrich - according to a poll for one of Israel's most popular newspapers, Yedioth Ahronoth.

And almost three-quarters see themselves as "right or centre-right", according to another survey for Israel's leading Channel 12 television network.

"Itamar Ben Gvir gives me a sense of security," said 20-year-old Mordechai, one of the young fans accompanying the politician to Ramle.

"Like everyone in history, from Trump to Moses, there are slips of the tongue that are a bit less good. So what? 90% of the things by Itamar are amazing."

"Itamar will give us safety, and when we go to the army, someone will have our backs and be behind us," said 18-year-old Nadav.

"I think he's trying to show that we're a strong country. For many years, we couldn't show we're strong in our beliefs. We couldn't express our ideology."

Meir Schreiber, an ultra-Orthodox 23-year-old who grew up in London, said the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks on Israel, which triggered the Gaza war, also convinced him that Ben Gvir was the right choice.

"Young people understand that peace isn't something we can do," he told me, "because what happens to you when you're young shapes your personality - we saw October 7."

Ben Gvir is a divisive candidate in a divided nation: his political positions include annexation of the occupied West Bank, Jewish settlement of Gaza, and the "voluntary emigration" of Palestinians - positions and rhetoric that are widely condemned by liberal Israelis.

Several Western countries have imposed sanctions or travel bans on Ben Gvir and Smotrich for incitement against Palestinians. Both men are powerful ministers in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's governing coalition.

As he and his entourage pushed their way between the stalls, some shopkeepers threw sweets; others, dark looks.

"I don't like him, he sows discord," one stallholder said. "Ramle is a mixed city - Jews and Arabs. There's no problem here, even after 7 October, but his message preys on young uneducated people."

The fact that he appears more popular with 18 to 22-year-olds than with their parents' generation is often put down, at least partly, to the impact of the 7 October attacks.

But political analyst Dahlia Scheindlin, who previously ran many Israeli political campaigns, said it was more than that.

"For about the last 20 years, we've seen young Israeli Jews are more right wing than average, and significantly more right-wing on many measures than the 55+ group," she told me.

"They have grown up under a series of wars with no personal experience of efforts to achieve peace. But for the most part, they have been socialised into the most extreme terms of the debate [as] legitimate to discuss: annexation, settlement expansion and - after 7 October - annexation of Gaza. And now they're voting for the first time."

A series of classroom debates filmed by Israeli satirist Lior Schleien recently highlighted the extreme views of some young Israelis.

The debates, in which he challenges racist or extreme views, drew a lot of attention in Israel, and included one exchange in which a student advocates killing all Arab citizens of Israel. That particular video has since been removed from Schleien's website.

Surveys suggest that first-time voters here are highly motivated to cast their ballots, with more than 80% saying they are likely to do so. But the same research suggests they are also more sceptical about democratic institutions and less engaged by political protests or petitions.

In a race that is largely deadlocked between two stable blocs of pro-government and anti-government supporters, getting new voters to the polling stations could make all the difference.

Opposition parties have been engaging younger voters with warnings about threats to democracy, new social media videos and younger candidates.

"In 2022 [in the last election], only 59% of the citizens living in Tel Aviv voted - in the most liberal city in the whole Middle East! In places where they voted for Ben Gvir, they voted at around 90%," said Yonatan Shalev, a 24-year-old candidate with the centre-right opposition party, Beyachad ("Together"), led by former prime minister Naftali Bennett.

He told me that Ben Gvir had understood the power of social media faster than other politicians.

"The liberal politicians didn't believe in TikTok, didn't believe in Instagram, and he took advantage of that arena."

Shalev said he had pushed his own party to reach young voters through social media.

"Three months ago, Ben Gvir was still the politician with the most amount of views on TikToks, the most amount of likes on TikTok, and Instagram as well," he explained. "Right now, Naftali Bennett is leading [that]."

His boss's Instagram page now features videos of the former prime minister lifting weights to rap music, or chatting with Shalev in the street. Even Netanyahu has joined in with a fast-paced militaristic social media video set to heavy beats.

"Younger people don't watch the news in Israel, [they] don't read the newspapers. The younger generation is getting all its details from TikTok and Instagram".

Yahlee Reske and Mika Magal, both 21 years old, rushed out of a nearby bar when they saw Shalev walk past.

"Yes," agreed Yahlee. "He's our age, he's so young and knows so much. It's hard to listen to people who are old and saying the same things over and over again."

Yahlee said she was doing national military service when the 7 October attacks unfolded.

"I don't think I ever looked at politics until then," she said. "But maybe if the government had been different on 7 October, things would have been better."

The same poll suggesting 16% of first-time voters would back a far-right party also suggested that Beyachad alone would take almost 9% of their votes, as would the centre-right Yashar party of Gadi Eisenkot.

At a student event in Tel Aviv last weekend, Ben Gvir was interrupted by protesters shouting, "Fascism will not pass", and forced off the stage.

Israel's young voters may be moving to the right, but they are still as divided as their country, over who they believe is the guardian of Israel's security and identity, and who is an existential threat.

articles.title: UK weather: Storm Austen named by Met Office as yellow wind warning issued
articles.summary: The first named storm of the season - Austen - will bring damaging winds and heavy rain to parts of the UK on Friday.
articles.body:
The first named storm of the autumn - Storm Austen - is set to batter parts of the UK with severe gales and heavy rain beginning from Thursday night.

Ahead of the storm, the Met Office has issued a yellow severe weather warning for wind, which will come into force at midnight Friday.

Damage to buildings and transport disruption is likely, with the possibility for power cuts.

While Storm Austen will move away later on Friday, another deep area of low pressure will bring more wet and windy weather on Saturday.

Over the next few days there willl be heavy rain across the UK, along with strengthening winds on Wednesday around west Wales and southern England.

But, it is from late on Thursday where a rapidly deepening area of low pressure - named Storm Austen by the Met Office - starts to approach from the Atlantic.

Heavy rain will move in across England and Wales through Thursday night accompanied by strengthening winds.

A Met Office yellow wind warning will be in force from midnight on Friday to 12:00 BST and covers south Wales, south-west England and along southern coastal counties of England.

Wind gusts of up to 70mph are expected which will likely bring damage to buildings, travel disruption and the risk of power cuts.

More widely gusts of 50-60mph will be felt around west Wales and through southern England.

While the strongest winds will ease from the south-west later on Friday morning, the rest of England and Wales will stay blustery with heavy rain at times through the day.

Scotland and Northern Ireland will largely miss any of the impacts caused by Storm Austen.

Storm Austen will clear away into the North Sea later on Friday and while there will be a quiet spell with clear skies overnight into Saturday, another area of low pressure will move in for the start of the weekend.

This deep area of low pressure - not expected to be as severe as Austen and therefore unlikely to be named - will head towards Scotland.

Gusts of 70-80mph will affect western Scotland with delays or cancellations to ferries and restrictions on bridges.

It will turn windy elsewhere across the UK throughout Saturday with heavy rain spreading east for most of us.

Sunday will turn drier but it will remain very wind, particularly towards the north east of Scotland.

articles.title: “I was denied entry to a temple for wearing shorts”: Meet Nehaa Bhatt, who lost a leg in a bus accident in 2021 but rebuilt her life with Ampu-Tea, dances Garba and takes on Himalayan pilgrimages with a prosthetic leg
articles.summary: “I am 80 percent disabled,” says Nehaa Bhatt, who is an inspiration for all those who say disability can stop them from living their dreams.
articles.body: “I am 80 percent disabled,” says Nehaa Bhatt, who is an inspiration for all those who say disability can stop them from living their dreams.Her story is not just about learning to walk again after losing a leg in an accident but it is about refusing to let her disability describe her life. Today, Nehaa runs a tea stall known as Ampu-Tea and also travels solo. She has undertaken some challenging pilgrimages with a prosthetic leg and refuses to let others take decisions for her. But her journey wasn’t easy. She also shares incidents which are painful reminders of how people with disabilities are judged.Who is Nehaa Bhatt?Bhatt was a schoolteacher with a secure future. Originally from Mahuva in Gujarat, she was working at a school in Gandhinagar. In November 2021, she met with an unfortunate road accident which changed her life overnight.As per her personal account, she was travelling on a Gujarat State Road Transport Corporation (GSRTC) bus from Ahmedabad towards Mahuva when it collided with a truck. She was seated in the front row and suffered severe injuries. Her injuries were so bad that doctors had to amputate her left leg.The accident disrupted her whole life, career and independence. With the accident went away the future she had imagined for herself. Her recovery was a difficult process. But gradually, she began looking for a way forward.When she was not allowed inside a templeHowever, Bhatt's experiences have not always been so happy or joyous.In August 2026, she described an incident at Ashapura Maa Temple in Jamnagar, Gujarat, where she said she was asked to leave the courtyard because she was wearing shorts. According to her account, she was not entering the main shrine but was standing in the outer courtyard so that she could see the temple from afar.She explained that wearing shorts allowed her to manage her prosthetic leg better. She also alleged that people made hurtful remarks about her disability, including describing it as the result of "bad karma". A pair of shorts might appear to be an ordinary clothing choice. For someone using a prosthetic limb, however, it is a practical and comfortable choice.Finding independence through a tea stallBhatt's first steps towards rebuilding her career was establishing a tea stall. After losing her teaching job, she decided to start a small business near Ahmedabad's Sabarmati Riverfront and named it Ampu-Tea, a play on the word "amputee". Her idea was to sell tea and earn a living. Her parents helped her, while crowdfunding and support from well-wishers helped her obtain a prosthetic leg.But her tea-selling journey had its setbacks. As per reports, her original tea stall was dismantled following intervention over its location, leaving her distressed. Later, she decided to travel and explore.Kedarnath, Amarnath trekFor many pilgrims, reaching Kedarnath is a dream as it involves a demanding mountain trek. For Bhatt with a prosthetic leg, the journey required much more. In September 2026, she completed the approximately 19-km trek to Kedarnath for a second time. Now her goal is to visit all 12 Jyotirlingas, and she had visited seven by then.In July 2026, another video from her Instagram attracted attention as she undertook the Amarnath Yatra via the Baltal route. The footage showed her moving along the rugged mountain trail with her prosthetic leg, a walking stick and a forearm crutch.Her journeys are proof that disability disappears when someone has a strong will and determination. A prosthetic limb does not remove pain, or the practical difficulties, but Bhatt's experiences show what becomes possible when a person is able to pursue an ambition.In October 2026, videos of her performing Garba with a prosthetic leg drew attention online. For Bhatt, the journey appears to be about more than reaching a destination. It is also about recovering the freedom to decide where she wants to go.Today, the name Ampu-Tea carries the story of a woman who turned a small cup of tea into a fresh beginning and continued to explore the world on her own terms.You use AI every day. articles.title: After a Louisiana priest admitted abusing his teenage son in 2018, deacon Scott Peyton left Catholic ministry and joined another church; the Vatican has now upheld his excommunication despite his appeal
articles.summary: A former Catholic deacon in Louisiana, who left the Church after a priest admitted sexually abusing his teenage son in 2018, has lost his appeal against
articles.body: A former Catholic deacon in Louisiana, who left the Church after a priest admitted sexually abusing his teenage son in 2018, has lost his appeal against excommunication. Scott Peyton, who resigned from Catholic ministry in 2023 and briefly joined an Anglican congregation, was informed that the Vatican had upheld his removal from the Catholic Church. The decision has drawn attention to the fact that Michael Guidry, the priest convicted of abusing Peyton's son, remains a priest despite serving a seven-year prison sentence.Peyton received the decision on Friday during a meeting with J Douglas Deshotel, the bishop of Lafayette. According to The Guardian, the Vatican's Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith (DDF) concluded that Peyton had formally separated himself from the Catholic Church by joining another Christian denomination.For Peyton, however, leaving the Church had followed years of distress over what happened to his family. He has maintained that he wanted to protect his family's faith while distancing himself from an institution whose handling of sexual abuse cases had deeply troubled him. He now worships with a nondenominational congregation.The ruling has also raised questions about the different actions taken against Peyton and Guidry. While Guidry was suspended from publicly carrying out priestly duties, he was not removed from the priesthood. Peyton, on the other hand, was excommunicated after changing churches. He has announced plans to challenge the Vatican's decision again.How case changed Peyton's relation with ChurchPeyton had been serving the Diocese of Lafayette since 2012. According to local news outlet Acadiana News First, he served alongside Guidry at St Peter Catholic Church in Morrow, Louisiana, where Peyton's son Oliver also served as an altar server.In 2018, Guidry admitted molesting Oliver, who was then a teenager. The priest was arrested, subsequently pleaded guilty and received a seven-year prison sentence. The Lafayette diocese also faced criticism after Guidry was given a farewell lunch by his church, prompting an apology from the diocese.The family later reached a $350,000 out-of-court settlement with the diocese in 2021. Peyton, his wife Letitia and Oliver subsequently became involved in supporting survivors of sexual abuse by clergy.Although Peyton continued his religious journey, he eventually decided that remaining a Catholic deacon was no longer possible. He resigned in December 2023, explaining his reasons in a letter to Bishop Deshotel."This decision is not a rejection of my faith in God or my commitment to living a life guided by Christian principles," he wrote as quoted by Acadiana News First.Peyton and his family then briefly attended an Anglican church. He also disclosed the move on social media. Within months, Deshotel issued a decree declaring that Peyton had separated himself from the Catholic Church and was excommunicated.Why Vatican upheld excommunicationPeyton challenged the decree in May 2024, arguing that the punishment served no useful religious purpose. He also said the decision had affected his wife and six children, who felt unwelcome in the Catholic Church.Excommunication is one of the most serious penalties under Catholic Church rules. It prevents a person from participating in certain sacraments, including receiving holy communion.The Vatican's DDF reviewed Peyton's appeal and rejected it on May 22, 2026. It nevertheless concluded that formally joining the Anglican church meant he had separated himself from the authority of the Catholic pope.The Vatican also observed that Bishop Deshotel could have warned Peyton more clearly about the consequences of joining another church. Despite that observation, it found the excommunication justified and expressed hope that reconciliation might eventually be possible.Peyton plans another appeal Following the decision, Peyton's lawyer, Dawn Eden Goldstein, said the bishop had confirmed that Guidry remained a Catholic priest. articles.body: A Canadian man serving a 40-year sentence for plotting terrorist attacks in New York City has been sentenced to another 50 years in prison after stabbing two correctional officers at a federal prison in Pennsylvania, leaving one permanently without his right eye.Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy, 28, was sentenced on Monday after pleading guilty to charges arising from the December 2020 attack at the US Penitentiary Allenwood, according to US Department of Justice. The additional term will run consecutively to his existing sentence, bringing his combined prison term to 90 years.Investigators said Bahnasawy attacked two officers on December 7 that year, using a weapon fashioned from part of a steel desk in his cell. He stabbed one officer in the head and face before attacking a second officer who came to help, injuring her hand. The first officer later lost his right eye as a result of the assault.A note found in Bahnasawy’s sock after he was restrained read: “This is a terrorist attack for the Islamic State.” Authorities also found a pledge of allegiance to the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham, commonly known as ISIS, taped inside a locker door in his cell.Assistant Attorney General John A Eisenberg said Bahnasawy had carried out the prison attack in the name of ISIS despite already serving time for an earlier terror conspiracy.“Today’s sentence will further ensure that Bahnasawy remains in prison, where he can do much less harm, for a very long time,” Eisenberg said.US Attorney Brian D Miller for the Middle District of Pennsylvania said the sentence reflected the government’s commitment to prosecuting people who commit violence on behalf of ISIS, including those who act from inside prison.FBI Counterterrorism Division Assistant Director Jarod Brown said the two officers survived the attack and stressed that violence motivated by ISIS or other foreign terrorist organisations would not be tolerated.Bahnasawy pleaded guilty in November last year to multiple charges, including assault, assault with intent to commit murder, possessing contraband in prison and providing material support to ISIS, which is designated a foreign terrorist organisation by the United States.His original 40-year sentence stemmed from a plan to carry out mass-casualty attacks in New York City in 2016. Bahnasawy, then 20, worked with Talha Haroon and Russell Salic on a conspiracy involving bombings and shootings in crowded areas during Ramadan, according to prosecutors.The FBI disrupted the plan after an undercover agent posed as an ISIS supporter willing to participate in the attacks. articles.title: UK to deploy jets to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
articles.summary: The UK announces it will provide additional defensive military support to Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate in the region.
articles.body:
The UK will deploy RAF Typhoon jets to defend Saudi Arabia in response to escalating Houthi missile and drone attacks, the defence secretary has said.

The defensive mission will help defend Saudi cities and infrastructure against aerial attacks by the Iran-backed group, Wes Streeting said in a written statement released on Tuesday.

It follows Houthi drone and ballistic missile attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh, as well as on energy sites on the country's coast.

"These aircraft will operate in a defensive role and will not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis," the statement adds.

The Houthis are locked in a civil war with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.

The UK will also deploy military advisers and an RAF A400M transport aircraft.

It is already providing Saudi Arabia with defence support equipment to protect against aerial attacks and air-to-air refuelling for defensive Saudi operations. The refuelling has now been extended by 90 days.

In a separate statement, Streeting said the targeting of Riyadh airport "shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region".

"That's why today I have approved further UK military support," the defence secretary added.

The Houthis have been launching missiles and drones at airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for the strikes on the territory that they control in western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.

articles.title: Strong storm winds could damage trees and disrupt Jersey travel
articles.summary: Forecasters say Jersey could be hit by the first named storm of the season at the end of the week.
articles.body:
Forecasters have warned that severe weather this week could bring tree branches down and disrupt travel.

Jersey Met has forecast that winds could reach severe gale force 9 by Friday morning, with gusts to 90mph (113km/h).

Senior forecaster Matt Winter said things could still change and forecasters were looking through several weather models to see what was most likely to happen.

He said: "At the moment, we are expecting to see gale perhaps severe gale-force winds... some of the model data has been suggesting we could see something a little bit stronger than that."

The island was hit by strong winds in Storm Goretti in January, and there was widespread damage when a tornado ripped through the east of the island during Storm Ciarán in 2023.

Ferry operator DFDS has rescheduled some services between Jersey, France and the UK ahead of the expected strong winds.

Winter said this week would see the first named storm of the season, which has now been called Storm Austen by the UK Met Office .

Winter said the majority of the week would see "unsettled" weather, with cooler temperatures, more rain and stronger winds.

He added that Jersey Met was reviewing the situation and would be talking to the government about what disruption the island could see.

He urged people to follow guidance and weather warnings.

He said they could be issued at short notice, but discussions with the government and emergency services would take place when there was potential for "a more impactful, severe storm".

articles.title: Hockenheim would stage F1 replacement race, if it opens door for more
articles.summary: Germany's Hockenheimring would be ready to step in and stage a Formula One race if tensions in the Middle East continue, but only under the condition that th...
articles.body:
Germany's Hockenheimring would be ready to step in and stage a Formula One race if tensions in the Middle East continue, but only under the condition that this would lead to a full return into the calendar.

Hockenheim managing directors Jörn Teske and Jochen Nerpel told the Formel.1 portal they were not interested in a one-off race.

"If this opportunity to host a replacement race opens the door significantly wider to a multi-year contract and a secure future in Formula 1, then that is certainly a scenario we will be giving a great deal of thought to," Teske said.

Staging a one-off replacement race would not be worth it, especially financially, as Nerpel said: "I can't imagine us just stepping in like that."

Hockenheim last hosted the German Grand Prix in 2019. The last race in the country came a year later at Nürburgring which stepped in during the coronavirus pandemic.

The Middle East hostilities led the cancellation of the races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, with the Bahrain race eventually held earlier this month in Malaysia. There are also question marks over the season-ending events in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, with Italy's Imola pencilled in as an alternative.

Hockenheim wants to return in principle but the hosting fee of around $20 million is a big obstacle. Nerpel said it was his "absolute wish" that F1 returns to Hockenheim, but there is nothing concrete on the matter at the moment.
